raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old male with a history of inflammatory colonic Crohn's disease diagnosed in 2017 underwent colonoscopy in September 2021 for disease assessment, which revealed endoscopically active colitis with a shallow ulcer in the rectum and a large circumferential patch of ulcerations in the right colon. The patient was then started on infliximab, an anti-TNF agent. After two induction doses of infliximab, the patient presented to the emergency department with cyclic fevers (101-104 F) for ten days. The patient experienced cramping right upper quadrant pain, night sweats, headaches, and shaking chills every evening with resolution of all symptoms during the day. He denied having any ill contacts or recent international travel. He had a history of international travel to Kuwait, Qatar, Egypt, Japan, and Italy in the early 2000s.
On examination, the patient was febrile (up to 101.8 F), mildly tachycardic (94 beats per minute), and on room air. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness on palpation of the right upper quadrant without rebound or guarding. Laboratory work was notable for leukocytosis (12.8 x 103/muL) with a mild elevation in neutrophil count (9.2 x 103/muL). Other pertinent labs are as follows: aspartate aminotransferase 50 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 49 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 71 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 18.2 seconds, international normalized ratio 1.75, and activated partial thromboplastin time 33.4 seconds. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis revealed two hypoenhancing lesions in the liver measuring 9.2 cm and 3.5 cm consistent with pyogenic liver abscesses (PLA) (Figures 1 and 2).
Chest radiography, urinalysis, and blood cultures results were unremarkable. Echinococcus and Entamoeba histolytica antigen tests were performed. CT-guided percutaneous abscess drainage with pigtail drain placement was also performed. Gram staining and culture of the liver abscess aspirate were negative. The patient was empirically treated with piperacillin/tazobactam for Gram-negative coverage of a suspected intraabdominal infection. On day seven of hospitalization, the Entamoeba histolytica enzyme immunoassay returned positive results. The patient was then treated with metronidazole for two weeks followed by one week of paromomycin therapy to eliminate any remaining intraluminal cysts. After one week of metronidazole therapy, stool antigen testing was negative for infection. The patient was subsequently examined in the clinic in January 2022 and had complete resolution of all symptoms while he was off infliximab treatment. In June 2022, the patient underwent a follow-up colonoscopy and was negative for endoscopically active disease. He will undergo a surveillance colonoscopy to monitor the recurrence of Crohn's disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male with inflammatory colonic Crohn's disease presented to the emergency department with a 10-day history of cyclic evening fevers (101-104 F), cramping right upper quadrant abdominal pain, night sweats, headaches, and shaking chills.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had undergone a disease-assessment colonoscopy in September 2021 showing endoscopically active colitis with a shallow rectal ulcer and a large circumferential patch of right colonic ulcerations, after which he was initiated on infliximab (anti-TNF therapy). Following two induction doses of infliximab, he developed cyclic fevers (101-104 F) lasting 10 days, accompanied by cramping right upper quadrant pain, night sweats, headaches, and shaking chills occurring every evening with complete daytime resolution of symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of inflammatory colonic Crohn's disease diagnosed in 2017. Remote international travel history to Kuwait, Qatar, Egypt, Japan, and Italy in the early 2000s.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cyclic fevers, shaking chills, night sweats, headaches, and cramping right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Denied ill contacts or recent international travel. Recent medication included infliximab (two induction doses).

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: febrile (temperature up to 101.8 F), mildly tachycardic (heart rate 94 beats/min), breathing comfortably on room air. Abdominal examination: mild tenderness on palpation of the right upper quadrant without rebound or guarding.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: leukocytosis (WBC 12.8 x 10^3/muL) with mild neutrophilia (9.2 x 10^3/muL). Liver function and coagulation tests: AST 50 IU/L, ALT 49 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 71 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, prothrombin time (PT) 18.2 seconds, INR 1.75, and aPTT 33.4 seconds. Chest radiography, urinalysis, and blood cultures were unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup: CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed two hypoenhancing liver lesions measuring 9.2 cm and 3.5 cm initially suspected to be pyogenic liver abscesses. CT-guided percutaneous abscess drainage with pigtail drain placement was performed; Gram stain and bacterial cultures of the liver abscess aspirate were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: On hospital day 7, Entamoeba histolytica enzyme immunoassay returned positive (Echinococcus testing and bacterial aspirate/blood cultures were negative), confirming amoebic liver abscess precipitated after anti-TNF (infliximab) induction. Initial empiric piperacillin/tazobactam was transitioned to targeted therapy with metronidazole for 2 weeks followed by intraluminal cyst eradication with paromomycin for 1 week, alongside percutaneous pigtail drainage and discontinuation of infliximab. Stool antigen testing was negative after 1 week of metronidazole; at clinic follow-up in January 2022 he had complete symptom resolution, and follow-up colonoscopy in June 2022 showed no endoscopically active Crohn's disease.
